Figure S5.1

Fitted hindsight-pathway chains

Note. Registered H1 model in the primary sample. Ten-item mean relevance mediates the likelihood route (H1a–H1b), and consequence severity mediates the foreseeability route (H1c–H1d). Path labels give unstandardized estimates in the original units, with robust (Huber–White) Wald 95% intervals. Outcome-to-mediator paths have separate Abortion (illegal abortion) and Disposal (improper disposal) estimates; relevance-to-likelihood and severity-to-foreseeability paths share estimates across contexts. Dashed paths have intervals containing zero for the shared estimate or for both context estimates. The tables report the indirect effects and omitted direct outcome paths, attitude slopes, and disturbance covariances. Expected evidence is evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion. Unexpected evidence is evidence of a financial crime. Each is compared with no information. Primary sample n per condition: illegal abortion, 68 with no information, 63 with expected evidence, and 63 with unexpected evidence; improper disposal, 71 with no information, 66 with expected evidence, and 67 with unexpected evidence. All 398 participants are in the analysis.

Table S5.9

Expected-evidence by item-consistency coefficient of the crossed mixed model: the registered ten-item analysis and the eight-item sensitivity analysis

Analysis Estimate SE df 95% CI Predicted Random structure Ratings Participants Decision
Note. Unstandardized coefficient in rating-scale points (items rated 1 to 9): the difference between consistent and inconsistent items in the expected-evidence minus no-information difference. Interval: two-sided 95% from the t distribution with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom and the REML fixed-effect covariance (Satterthwaite t, REML fixed-effect covariance); no bootstrap is used in this analysis. Sensitivity analysis (deviations record, item 1; not registered and not a support criterion): the same model, the same fallback sequence for the random structure, and the same interval on items 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, without the background items 3 and 10. Figure S5.5

Mean rated relevance of each evidence item after no information and after outcome information

Note. Points are the mean observed relevance ratings (1 to 9) of each item, with the two legal contexts weighted equally. Each line runs from the mean after no information to the mean after the outcome information in that panel. I show the means without intervals here. The item-difference table gives the differences and their unadjusted Welch 95% intervals. Table S5.9 gives the registered coefficient. Expected evidence is evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion. Unexpected evidence is evidence of a financial crime. Each is compared with no information. Primary sample n per condition: illegal abortion, 68 with no information, 63 with expected evidence, and 63 with unexpected evidence; improper disposal, 71 with no information, 66 with expected evidence, and 67 with unexpected evidence. All 398 participants are in the analysis.

Figure S5.6

Model-predicted relevance of the outcome-consistent and outcome-inconsistent items after each kind of outcome information

Note. I used the mixed model to predict relevance ratings on the 1 to 9 scale. The points compare items consistent with expected evidence (i.e., 1, 6, and 7) with inconsistent items (i.e., 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, and 10) under each outcome-information condition. I set the random effects to zero to obtain population means, holding attitudes at their participant means and weighting the legal contexts equally. The bars describe uncertainty in each mean: normal-based 95% intervals calculated by the delta method from the REML fixed-effect covariance. Their overlap does not test E4a. The registered comparison is the change in the difference between item sets from no information to expected evidence, reported in Table S5.9. Expected evidence is evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion. Unexpected evidence is evidence of a financial crime. Each is compared with no information. Primary sample n per condition: illegal abortion, 68 with no information, 63 with expected evidence, and 63 with unexpected evidence; improper disposal, 71 with no information, 66 with expected evidence, and 67 with unexpected evidence. All 398 participants are in the analysis.
